newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-SAMPRAS SQUEAKS INTO PHILADELPHIA FINAL.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SAMPRAS SQUEAKS INTO PHILADELPHIA FINAL.

text.p: World number one Pete Sampras had to scramble to win a marathon 3-6 7-5 6-3 semifinal Saturday against qualifier Sjeng Schalken of the Netherlands at the $714,250 Advanta Championships.

But the match, the first to captivate the crowd this week, ended on a sour note. After the two players duked it out for two hours, it was one of five foot-faults in the match that ended the day for the 88th-ranked Schalken.
The fans booed when Schalken was called for a second-serve foot-fault on the last point of the match.
"We played really good tennis," Sampras said. "To end it like that is not really fair."
Sampras, who has a 16-0 winning streak for the year and a 19-0 overall streak going, will play 60th-ranked Patrick Rafter of Australia in an attempt to win his third Philadelphia title.
Rafter, who has beaten Sampras once in their four career meetings, captured a 6-3 6-4 semifinal win over 78th-ranked Grant Stafford of South Africa.
"My intention today was to go out there and give 100 percent," said Rafter, who has been receiving acupuncture on his right elbow all week. "I played my butt off and I think Grant did, too."
Despite the odd ending, Schalken could walk away from the match proud of his performance -- he kept the world's best player on the ropes.
"It was nice for me," Schalken said. "It was a lot more fun than the last time. I was feeling I had a little chance."
The last time the two played, at the 1996 Lipton Championships, Schalken won only five games.
Sampras asserted himself in the eighth game of the second set with Schalken ahead 4-3.
Sampras saved two break points in that game to even the score 4-4. If he had lost his serve, Schalken would have been serving for the match at 5-3.
"I raised my level when I had to or he would've been serving for the match," said Sampras, who made 47 unforced errors in the match. "The way he was playing, he was going to play it out there."
Schalken consistently hit big enough to keep the American uncharacteristically pinned to the baseline.
Most players have difficulty breaking Sampras's serve once. Schalken was successful on five of 10 opportunities.

"He was playing the type of tennis that gets you into the top 10, top 15," Sampras said. "He wasn't making errors. I was the one making or breaking points. He played well enough to beat me. I just managed to squeak this one out."
In the first set, Schalken raced to a 5-1 lead and lost only one point in his first three service games.
"I was surprised I won the first set," Schalken said. "I was playing all the time to his backhand. If you play to his forehand, it's about almost always over."
After exchanging early service breaks in the second set, Sampras broke serve in the 11th game courtesy of a number of Schalken errors.
Two service breaks in the fifth and seventh games of the final set put Sampras ahead 5-2 and serving for the match.
Schalken made a last stab at staying alive, breaking Sampras's serve in the eighth game.
Rafter, looking for his second career title, broke Stafford's serve twice to the South African's once in the first set.
In the second set, Rafter scored the one service break at 15-40 in the seventh game.
